error_modes.label: ALTITUDE CONTROL WITHIN THE ASSIGNED AREA BLOCK

texts.0: SP, due to an altimeter cross-check that was interrupted while maneuvering inside the area, did not remain within the altitudes assigned for the flight. Altitude excursions exceeded 300 feet from the assigned value and the aircraft left the upper limit of the assigned block unrecognized. IP intervention on the controls was required to reestablish the aircraft in the assigned altitude block.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that stayed outside the cockpit during repositioning within the area, did not maintain the assigned area altitude with the required precision. Deviations reached 300 feet, at the limit of the allowable tolerance, and were held there without being recognized. Correction was initiated only after verbal prompting from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power correction on rolling out of the turn, did not hold the assigned area altitude exactly. Deviations reached approximately 200 feet, between the 150 foot and the 300 foot tolerance. SP identified the trend on the altimeter and returned to the assigned altitude in good time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP remained within the altitudes assigned for the flight throughout the working phase, with deviations contained inside 150 feet. Corrections were small, prompt and applied with smooth pitch and power inputs. The altimeter stayed inside the cross-check while maneuvering in the area.
texts.4: SP held the assigned area altitude with negligible deviations, well inside 150 feet and for most of the sortie within a few tens of feet. Corrections were anticipatory rather than reactive, applied before any trend could develop. Altitude control was unaffected by the demands of the maneuvering being flown.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the altitude standard for the assigned area, but the deviations were consistently near the upper edge of the tolerance and were corrected late. The trend indicates an altimeter check made at long intervals while maneuvering. SP is expected to shorten the cross-check interval so that altitude is held comfortably inside the tolerance rather than close to its limit.

texts_at.0: SP flew within the assigned altitude block with the IP calling the cross-check interval needed while maneuvering in the area, due to first exposure to holding an altimeter scan through continuous maneuvering rather than in straight and level flight. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to hold the assigned area altitude independently on the next sortie, without the cross-check interval being called.
texts_at.1: SP remained within the altitudes assigned for the area to the level expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 300 feet, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the altimeter cross-check interval being longer than the rate of maneuvering in the area allowed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to shorten the altimeter cross-check interval to match the rate of maneuvering being flown.
texts_at.2: SP identified the trend on the altimeter and returned to the assigned altitude in good time, correcting a deviation of about 200 feet, due to a late power correction on rolling out of the turn. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the power correction as the roll-out begins rather than after it is complete.
texts_at.3: SP remained within the altitudes assigned for the flight with deviations contained inside about 150 feet, due to one correction being applied a beat later than the trend first appeared on the altimeter. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to act on the altimeter trend the instant it appears rather than a beat later.

texts_above.1: SP remained within the altitudes assigned for the area with the deviation reaching about 270 feet, near the upper part of the tolerance, before the trend was corrected on the altimeter. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a deviation of about 200 feet developing after a late power correction on rolling out of a turn and returned to the assigned altitude in good time, with no intervention. Applying the power correction as the roll-out begins, rather than after it is complete, would remove the deviation before it develops. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good area-altitude control.
texts_above.3: SP remained within the altitudes assigned for the flight throughout the working phase, with deviations contained inside about 110 feet, corrections small, prompt and applied with smooth pitch and power inputs while the altimeter stayed inside the cross-check. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good area-altitude technique.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned area altitude with deviations of a few tens of feet, corrections anticipatory rather than reactive and applied before any trend could develop, altitude control unaffected by the demands of the maneuvering being flown. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent area-altitude control.

texts.0: SP, due to power settings applied without reference to the airspeed indicator during repositioning in the area, did not maintain the airspeed required for the assigned profile. Airspeed deviations exceeded 20 knots and were allowed to persist while the aircraft tracked toward the area boundary. IP intervention was required to reset power and recover the target airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to attention concentrated on the outside area references, did not control airspeed with the required precision while working in the area. Deviations reached 20 knots, at the limit of the allowable tolerance, and remained unrecognized. Power was corrected only after the IP called the airspeed.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting left unchanged after the change of pitch attitude, did not hold the target airspeed exactly. Deviations reached approximately 15 knots, between the 10 knot and the 20 knot tolerance. SP noted the divergence and reset power in good time, with no intervention required.
texts.3: SP controlled airspeed accurately while working in the assigned area, with deviations contained inside 10 knots. Power changes were anticipated for each attitude and configuration change. Airspeed remained inside the cross-check throughout the maneuvering.
texts.4: SP held the target airspeed with negligible deviations, well inside 10 knots for the entire working phase. Power was set precisely for each attitude change so that no correction was needed after the fact. Airspeed control remained stable even while position relative to the area boundary was being assessed.
texts.marginal: SP kept airspeed within the standard for the assigned area, but the deviations sat close to the tolerance and were corrected only after they had developed. The trend shows power being set by feel rather than confirmed against the indicator. SP is expected to confirm each power setting against the airspeed indication so that the margin to the tolerance increases.

texts_at.0: SP flew the area work with the IP calling the power setting needed each time the pitch attitude changed, due to first exposure to folding a power check into a scan already occupied by the outside area references. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to control airspeed while working in the area independently on the next sortie, without the power setting being called.
texts_at.1: SP controlled airspeed while working in the area to the level expected at this stage, with the deviation reaching about 20 knots, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to attention concentrated on the outside area references leaving the power setting unchecked for longer than the maneuvering allowed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to fold a power check into the outside scan rather than treating the two as separate tasks.
texts_at.2: SP noted the divergence and reset power in good time, correcting a deviation of about 15 knots, due to a power setting left unchanged after a change of pitch attitude. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to adjust power in the same action as the pitch change rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP controlled airspeed accurately while working in the assigned area, with deviations contained inside about 10 knots, due to one power change being anticipated a beat later than the attitude change that required it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate the power change at the same moment as the attitude change, not a beat after.

texts_above.1: SP controlled airspeed while working in the area with the deviation reaching about 18 knots before power was reset to recover the target value. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP noted an airspeed divergence of about 15 knots after a pitch attitude change and reset power in good time, with no intervention required. Adjusting power in the same action as the pitch change, rather than after it, would remove the divergence before it develops. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound area-airspeed management.
texts_above.3: SP controlled airspeed accurately while working in the assigned area, with deviations contained inside about 8 knots, power changes anticipated for each attitude and configuration change so airspeed remained inside the cross-check throughout the maneuvering. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed area-airspeed technique.
texts_above.4: SP held the target airspeed with deviations of two or three knots for the entire working phase, power set precisely for each attitude change so no correction was needed after the fact even while position relative to the boundary was being assessed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional area-airspeed control.

error_modes.label: EXIT HEADING ACCURACY ON DEPARTING THE AREA

texts.0: SP, due to a rollout begun without reference to the required exit heading, did not depart the assigned area on the heading briefed for the recovery. The heading error exceeded 10 degrees and the aircraft tracked toward an adjacent area rather than toward the recovery point. IP intervention was required to establish the correct exit heading.
texts.1: SP, due to a rate of roll not adjusted for the remaining turn, did not achieve the exit heading with the required precision. The heading error settled at 10 degrees, at the limit of the allowable tolerance, and was maintained without recognition. SP corrected onto the exit heading only after verbal prompting from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start of the rollout from the exit turn, did not roll out exactly on the required heading. The overshoot reached approximately 8 degrees, between the 5 degree and the 10 degree tolerance. SP recognized the error against the HSI and corrected onto the exit heading promptly without intervention.
texts.3: SP departed the assigned area on the required exit heading with an error contained inside 5 degrees. The rollout was anticipated and the heading was captured directly, without subsequent hunting. The exit was flown with the recovery track already established.
texts.4: SP rolled out on the required exit heading with negligible error, well inside 5 degrees. The lead point for the rollout was judged accurately and the heading was captured on the first attempt. The area was left on a track that required no further correction.
texts.marginal: SP achieved the required exit heading within the standard, but the rollout was consistently short of the target and the final capture was made in small stages. The trend indicates that the lead point is being judged reactively rather than computed from the turn rate. SP is expected to anticipate the rollout so that the exit heading is captured directly and with a wider margin to the tolerance.

texts_at.0: SP departed the assigned area with the IP calling the rate of roll needed for the amount of turn remaining to the exit heading, due to first exposure to judging a rollout rate against a heading rather than a general direction of travel. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to depart the area on the required exit heading independently on the next sortie, without the rate of roll being called.
texts_at.1: SP achieved the exit heading on departing the area to the level expected at this stage, with the error settling about 10 degrees, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the rate of roll not being adjusted for the amount of turn remaining. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to adjust the rate of roll to the turn remaining rather than holding one fixed rate.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the error against the HSI and corrected onto the exit heading promptly, correcting an overshoot of about 8 degrees, due to a late start of the rollout from the exit turn. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to begin the rollout from the lead point computed for the turn rather than starting it late.
texts_at.3: SP departed the assigned area on the required exit heading with an error contained inside about 5 degrees, due to the rollout lead being judged a shade short for the bank being carried, though captured directly. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the rollout lead to the actual bank angle being flown.

texts_above.1: SP departed the assigned area with the heading error reaching about 8 degrees before the rollout was corrected onto the required exit heading. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized an overshoot of about 8 degrees on the exit turn caused by a late rollout start and corrected onto the exit heading promptly against the HSI, with no intervention. Beginning the rollout from the lead point computed for the turn, rather than starting it late, would remove the overshoot before it appears. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid exit-heading technique.
texts_above.3: SP departed the assigned area on the required exit heading with an error contained inside about 4 degrees, the rollout anticipated and the heading captured directly without subsequent hunting, the exit flown with the recovery track already established. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed exit-heading control.
texts_above.4: SP rolled out on the required exit heading with error of about a degree, the lead point for the rollout judged accurately and the heading captured on the first attempt, the area left on a track that required no further correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding exit-heading control.

error_modes.label: LATERAL CONTAINMENT AND ADJACENT AREA VIOLATION

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the area boundary, violated the adjacent flight area without authorization. The aircraft continued approximately two miles past the boundary before any deviation was recognized, with altitude also outside the assigned block by more than 300 feet. IP intervention was required to turn the aircraft back into the assigned area.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the area boundary, did not maintain a working margin inside the assigned area. The aircraft was flown along the boundary with essentially no lateral margin and the altitude sat at the 300 foot limit of the tolerance. SP turned back toward the center of the area only after the IP called the proximity to the boundary.
texts.2: SP, due to lack of awareness of the closure rate toward the area boundary during the maneuvering, allowed the lateral margin to reduce below that briefed. The aircraft came within about one mile of the boundary with altitude deviating some 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP identified the closure on the navigation display and turned back inside the area in good time, with no intervention required.
texts.3: SP recognized and maintained the assigned area throughout the sortie and did not violate any adjacent flight area. Maneuvering was planned so that each turn was completed with a comfortable lateral margin to the boundary, and the assigned altitudes were held inside 150 feet. Position relative to the boundary was checked before each new maneuver.
texts.4: SP maintained the assigned area with negligible erosion of the lateral margin, positioning every maneuver in the working portion of the area rather than near its edges. Adjacent areas were never approached and the assigned altitudes were held with deviations of a few tens of feet. Area boundaries were tracked continuously without any prompting.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the assigned flight area, but the maneuvering was repeatedly completed close to the boundary and the recovery turns were started late. The trend shows the boundary being used as a limit rather than as a margin. SP is expected to plan the maneuvering so that each sequence finishes well inside the area, restoring the buffer against an inadvertent violation.

texts_at.0: SP maintained the assigned flight area with the IP calling the closure rate toward the nearest boundary through the maneuvering, due to first exposure to judging closure toward a boundary that has no ground feature marking it. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to maintain the assigned area independently on the next sortie, without the closure rate being called.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the assigned flight area to the level expected at this stage, with altitude reaching about 300 feet from the block and the lateral margin at its narrowest during the maneuvering, due to the closure rate toward the boundary being checked less often than the rate of maneuvering required. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the closure rate toward the boundary at the same rate the maneuvering is flown, not on a fixed interval.
texts_at.2: SP identified the closure on the navigation display and turned back inside the area in good time, correcting an approach to about one mile from the boundary with altitude deviating about 200 feet, due to a lack of awareness of the closure rate during the maneuvering. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check the closure rate immediately after every maneuver, not only when the margin has already narrowed.
texts_at.3: SP recognized and maintained the assigned area throughout the sortie with altitude held inside about 150 feet, due to one maneuver being planned with a lateral margin a shade narrower than the others, though still comfortable. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to plan every maneuver with the same generous margin, not only most of them.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the assigned flight area, with the lateral margin narrowed and altitude reaching about 270 feet from the block before the closure was checked and the aircraft turned back toward the center. The check followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a closure toward the boundary to about one mile with altitude deviating about 200 feet, checked the navigation display and turned back inside the area in good time, with no intervention. Checking the closure rate immediately after every maneuver, rather than only when the margin has already narrowed, would remove the correction from the working area. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady area-containment discipline.
texts_above.3: SP recognized and maintained the assigned area throughout the sortie, planning maneuvering so that each turn was completed with a comfortable lateral margin to the boundary and the assigned altitudes held inside about 110 feet, position relative to the boundary checked before each new maneuver. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate area-containment technique.
texts_above.4: SP maintained the assigned area with negligible erosion of the lateral margin, positioning every maneuver in the working portion of the area rather than near its edges, assigned altitudes held with deviations of a few tens of feet and area boundaries tracked continuously without any prompting. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary area-containment discipline.

error_modes.label: AREA CHARACTERISTIC POINTS AND ASSIGNED ALTITUDE BLOCK

texts.0: SP, due to an area study not completed during mission planning, was not aware of the flight area characteristic points and the altitudes assigned for the flight. SP could not identify the reference points defining the area and flew more than 300 feet outside the assigned altitude block. IP had to state the area limits and take control to reposition the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to characteristic points memorized as names rather than associated with ground features, was not able to relate the aircraft position to the area reference points without assistance. The altitude was held at the 300 foot limit of the block tolerance. SP established the correct picture of the area only after the IP identified the reference points verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow association between the area chart and the terrain below, was not immediately aware of which characteristic point defined the sector being worked. Altitude within the block deviated approximately 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP resolved the picture using the chart and the visible features in good time and without intervention.
texts.3: SP was aware of the flight area characteristic points and remained within the altitudes assigned for the flight. The reference points were identified without hesitation and used to orient the maneuvering, with altitude held inside 150 feet of the assigned block. The area picture was maintained throughout the working phase.
texts.4: SP demonstrated a complete picture of the area, naming the characteristic points and their relative bearings without reference to the chart and holding the assigned altitudes with negligible deviation. Maneuvering was oriented on those points so that position was continuously known. The altitude block was respected with margin at both its upper and lower limits.
texts.marginal: SP was aware of the area characteristic points and stayed within the assigned altitudes, but each identification required a deliberate pause and a chart reference before the maneuvering resumed. The trend shows an area picture that is being reconstructed rather than retained. SP is expected to study the area before flight so that the reference points are recognized immediately and attention stays with the aircraft.

texts_at.0: SP oriented on the flight area characteristic points with the IP identifying each reference point and its ground feature in turn, due to first exposure to associating the area chart with the terrain rather than reading the chart alone. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to identify the area characteristic points independently on the next sortie, without the reference points being called.
texts_at.1: SP was aware of the flight area characteristic points and remained within the altitudes assigned for the flight to the level expected at this stage, with altitude deviation reaching about 300 feet, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to characteristic points being associated with ground features a beat slower than the maneuvering required. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to fix each characteristic point against its ground feature during mission planning, before it is needed in the air.
texts_at.2: SP resolved the picture using the chart and the visible features in good time, correcting an altitude deviation of about 200 feet, due to a slow association between the area chart and the terrain below for one reference point. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to rehearse the chart-to-terrain association for every characteristic point before the sortie, not only the ones expected to be used.
texts_at.3: SP was aware of the flight area characteristic points and remained within the altitudes assigned for the flight, with altitude held inside about 150 feet, due to one reference point being identified a moment after it was reached rather than in anticipation of it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate each characteristic point before it is reached rather than identifying it on arrival.

texts_above.1: SP oriented on the flight area characteristic points, with altitude reaching about 270 feet from the assigned block before the chart-to-terrain picture was resolved. The resolution followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP resolved a slow chart-to-terrain association for one reference point using the chart and the visible features in good time, correcting an altitude deviation of about 200 feet with no intervention. Rehearsing the chart-to-terrain association for every characteristic point before the sortie, rather than only when one is slow to resolve, would remove the correction from the area work. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable area-orientation technique.
texts_above.3: SP was aware of the flight area characteristic points and remained within the altitudes assigned for the flight, reference points identified without hesitation and used to orient the maneuvering, altitude held inside about 110 feet of the assigned block throughout the working phase. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good area-orientation technique.
texts_above.4: SP demonstrated a complete picture of the area, naming the characteristic points and their relative bearings without reference to the chart and holding the assigned altitudes with deviations of a few tens of feet, maneuvering oriented on those points so position was continuously known. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior area-orientation technique.

error_modes.label: POSITION CONFIRMATION USING VOR/TACAN OR GPS

texts.0: SP, due to reliance on the automated navigation solution in place of a positive position fix, was not able to use VOR/TACAN or GPS to confirm the aircraft position when required. SP did not extract a radial and distance from the area reference point, and the position stated was in error by more than five miles. IP had to take over the navigation task to reestablish the aircraft within the assigned area.
texts.1: SP, due to acceptance of the automated navigation display without an independent check of the parameters, did not confirm the aircraft position with the required accuracy. The radial and distance were read incorrectly and the resulting position error placed the aircraft at the edge of the assigned area, with heading also at the 10 degree limit of the tolerance. SP obtained a valid fix only after the IP directed the correct selection.
texts.2: SP, due to a navigation source selected but not verified against the expected indications, was slow to confirm the aircraft position from VOR/TACAN. The initial fix contained an error of a few miles and the exit heading derived from it was off by approximately 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degree tolerance. SP cross-checked against GPS, corrected the fix and the heading in good time, without intervention.
texts.3: SP used VOR/TACAN and GPS correctly to confirm the aircraft position within the assigned area. The equipment was selected and identified before use, and the radial and distance were read accurately, giving an exit heading within 5 degrees of that required. Position was confirmed without interrupting the control of the aircraft.
texts.4: SP confirmed the aircraft position with negligible error, cross-checking the GPS position against the VOR/TACAN radial and distance without prompting and without any degradation of aircraft control. Each fix was obtained quickly and the results were integrated directly into the area maneuvering plan. Navigation displays were used as a check on the visual picture rather than as a substitute for it.
texts.marginal: SP was able to confirm position using VOR/TACAN or GPS, but each fix required a long head-down interval and altitude drifted toward the edge of the tolerance during it. The trend shows the position check being treated as a separate task rather than folded into the cross-check. SP is expected to break the navigation check into short looks so that aircraft control and area awareness are maintained throughout.

texts_at.0: SP confirmed the aircraft position using VOR/TACAN or GPS with the IP calling the expected radial and distance before the fix was accepted, due to first exposure to cross-checking a navigation source against the expected indication rather than accepting the display directly. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to confirm the aircraft position independently on the next sortie, without the expected indication being called.
texts_at.1: SP confirmed the aircraft position using VOR/TACAN or GPS to the level expected at this stage, with the resulting exit heading about 10 degrees off, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the navigation source being read but not cross-checked against the expected indications before the fix was used. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check the navigation source against the expected indication before using the fix, not after.
texts_at.2: SP cross-checked against GPS, corrected the fix and the heading in good time, correcting an exit heading error of about 7 degrees, due to a navigation source that was selected but not verified against the expected indications before the initial fix was read. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to verify the navigation source against the expected indication as the first step of every fix, before the reading is used.
texts_at.3: SP used VOR/TACAN and GPS correctly to confirm the aircraft position, with the resulting exit heading held to within about 3 to 4 degrees, due to the equipment being identified a beat after selection rather than as part of the same action. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to identify the equipment in the same action as selecting it, not as a following step.

texts_above.1: SP confirmed the aircraft position using VOR/TACAN or GPS, with the resulting exit heading about 8 degrees off before the fix was cross-checked and the heading corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a navigation source that had been selected but not verified against the expected indications, cross-checked against GPS, corrected the fix and the heading in good time, holding the resulting error to about 7 degrees with no intervention. Verifying the navigation source against the expected indication as the first step of every fix, rather than after an unverified reading is used, would remove the correction from the transit. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured position-fixing technique.
texts_above.3: SP used VOR/TACAN and GPS correctly to confirm the aircraft position within the assigned area, the equipment selected and identified before use with the radial and distance read accurately, giving an exit heading within about 3 to 4 degrees of that required. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise position-fixing technique.
texts_above.4: SP confirmed the aircraft position with negligible error, cross-checking the GPS position against the VOR/TACAN radial and distance without prompting and without any degradation of aircraft control, each fix obtained quickly and integrated directly into the area maneuvering plan. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate position-fixing technique.

error_modes.label: RETURN TO BASE AND DIVERSION DECISION

texts.0: SP, due to mission-completion bias in pressing on past the briefed decision point, did not initiate the return to base while the conditions still permitted a safe recovery. The area was left below the briefed recovery fuel and without a diversion to the alternate airfield being considered. IP had to direct and then fly the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to mission-completion bias that overrode the briefed divert criteria, did not initiate the return to base at the planned point. The recovery was begun with the fuel at the briefed minimum and the exit heading toward base in error by 10 degrees, at the limit of the tolerance. SP started the RTB only after being prompted by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on completing the last sequence in the area, was late in initiating the return to base. The recovery started after the planned time, with the exit heading approximately 8 degrees off, between the 5 and 10 degree tolerance, and the altitude some 200 feet from that assigned. SP recognized the delay, made the RTB decision unprompted and corrected the profile in good time.
texts.3: SP returned to base safely and at the briefed point, having monitored fuel and time against the criteria set in the brief. The area was left on the required exit heading within 5 degrees and at the assigned altitude within 150 feet. SP stated the intentions for the recovery and the alternate airfield without prompting.
texts.4: SP managed the sortie so that the return to base was initiated with margin against every briefed criterion, and was able to state the current diversion option and the fuel required for it at any point. The area was left with negligible deviation in heading and altitude. The recovery decision was made deliberately and communicated before it was executed.
texts.marginal: SP returned to base safely and within the criteria, but the decision was taken at the last of the briefed decision points and left little margin against the alternate. The trend shows the recovery being treated as the end of the working phase rather than as a planned event with its own criteria. SP is expected to track fuel and weather against the divert criteria continuously so that the RTB decision is made with margin in hand.

texts_at.0: SP initiated the return to base with the IP calling the divert criteria against fuel and time as the planned decision point approached, due to first exposure to weighing the RTB decision against fixed criteria rather than against the progress of the last sequence in the area. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to make the RTB decision independently on the next sortie, without the divert criteria being called.
texts_at.1: SP initiated the return to base to the level expected at this stage, with the exit heading toward base about 10 degrees off and altitude about 300 feet from that assigned, due to attention held on completing the last sequence in the area rather than on the RTB criteria as the decision point approached. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the RTB criteria on a fixed schedule that does not depend on whether the last sequence has been finished.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the delay, made the RTB decision unprompted and corrected the profile in good time, with the exit heading about 7 degrees off and altitude about 200 feet from that assigned, due to attention being held on completing the last sequence in the area. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make the RTB decision at the planned point regardless of how the last sequence in the area is progressing.
texts_at.3: SP returned to base safely and at the briefed point, with the exit heading held within about 3 to 4 degrees and altitude within about 150 feet, due to the fuel and time check being made a beat after the planned decision point rather than exactly at it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check fuel and time exactly at the planned decision point, not a beat after.

texts_above.1: SP initiated the return to base, with the exit heading toward base about 8 degrees off and altitude about 270 feet from that assigned before the RTB decision was made and the profile corrected. The decision followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a late return-to-base decision caused by attention held on completing the last sequence in the area, made the RTB decision unprompted and corrected the profile in good time, with the exit heading held to about 7 degrees and altitude to about 200 feet, with no intervention. Making the RTB decision at the planned point regardless of the last sequence's progress, rather than after it is finished, would remove the correction from the recovery. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent RTB decision-making.
texts_above.3: SP returned to base safely and at the briefed point, having monitored fuel and time against the criteria set in the brief, the area left on the required exit heading within about 3 to 4 degrees and at the assigned altitude within about 110 feet, intentions for the recovery and the alternate airfield stated without prompting. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined RTB decision-making.
texts_above.4: SP managed the sortie so the return to base was initiated with margin against every briefed criterion, able to state the current diversion option and fuel required for it at any point, the area left with negligible deviation in heading and altitude and the recovery decision made deliberately and communicated before it was executed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless RTB decision-making.

error_modes.label: CENTER RADIAL METHOD SETUP AND CDI INTERPRETATION

texts.0: SP set the reciprocal of the center radial in the course selector window, so the course arrow pointed towards the NAVAID when the center radial was intended, and then steered away from the CDI. The rule that the center of the area is always toward the CDI was applied in reverse and the aircraft tracked outside the lateral limits, with altitude also more than 300 feet out of the assigned block. IP intervened to reset the course selector window and turn the aircraft back into the area.
texts.1: SP set the center radial in the course selector window but read the CDI as a raw bearing indication rather than as the direction of the area center, so no correction was flown toward the deflected bar. The aircraft drifted onto the edge of the area with altitude sitting at the 300 foot limit of the tolerance. SP turned back toward the center of the area only after the IP called the CDI indication.
texts.2: SP set the center radial correctly but was slow to reapply the toward the CDI rule after a reversal turn, so the drift toward the boundary was identified late. The aircraft closed to the edge of the working portion of the area and altitude deviated some 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP rechecked the course arrow and CDI without prompting and re-centered the aircraft in the area in good time.
texts.3: SP set the center radial of the area in the course selector window so the course arrow pointed away from the NAVAID, and used the CDI deflection to keep the area center identified throughout the sortie. Lateral position was held with a working margin to both boundaries and altitude stayed inside 150 feet of the assigned block. The setup was rechecked after each reversal turn.
texts.4: SP set the center radial in the course selector window before entering the area and used the CDI as a continuous lateral reference, keeping every maneuver in the working portion of the area. Altitude was held within a few tens of feet of the assigned block. No re-setting of the reference and no prompting were required at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP kept the center radial method set and remained within the area, but the CDI was consulted only after a drift toward one boundary had already developed. The trend is a lateral position that is recovered reactively instead of being maintained, with each reversal starting closer to the edge. SP is expected to read the CDI as part of the routine crosscheck so that the area center is regained before the margin erodes.

texts_at.0: SP set the center radial method with the IP calling the toward-the-CDI rule each time it needed to be reapplied after a reversal turn, due to first exposure to reading the CDI as a continuous area-center reference rather than as a raw bearing indication. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to apply the center radial method independently on the next sortie, without the toward-the-CDI rule being called.
texts_at.1: SP set the center radial method and used the CDI to keep the area center identified to the level expected at this stage, with altitude deviation reaching about 300 feet, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the toward-the-CDI rule being reapplied a beat later than the reversal turn required. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reapply the toward-the-CDI rule the instant the reversal turn is complete, not a beat after.
texts_at.2: SP rechecked the course arrow and CDI without prompting and re-centered the aircraft in the area in good time, correcting an altitude deviation of about 200 feet, due to being slow to reapply the toward-the-CDI rule after a reversal turn. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to build the CDI recheck into the reversal turn itself as its final step.
texts_at.3: SP set the center radial of the area in the course selector window and used the CDI deflection to keep the area center identified, altitude held inside about 150 feet, due to the setup being rechecked a beat after the reversal turn rather than as part of it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to recheck the setup as the last action of every reversal turn.

texts_above.1: SP set the center radial method, with altitude reaching about 270 feet from the assigned block before the toward-the-CDI rule was reapplied and the aircraft re-centered. texts_above.2: SP recognized being slow to reapply the toward-the-CDI rule after a reversal turn, rechecked the course arrow and CDI without prompting and re-centered the aircraft with altitude held to about 200 feet, with no intervention. Building the CDI recheck into the reversal turn itself, rather than after it is complete, would remove the correction from the area work. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good center-radial technique.

Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good center-radial technique.

error_modes.label: PIE IN THE SKY BOUNDARY SETUP AND BEARING POINTER CONTAINMENT

texts.0: SP marked only one of the two area boundaries, setting the boundary course in the course selector window but leaving the heading marker on the previous heading instead of on the other boundary course. With no second reference the head of the bearing pointer was allowed to fall past the unmarked boundary and the aircraft entered the adjacent area, with altitude also more than 300 feet out of the assigned block. IP intervened to re-establish the aircraft inside the assigned area.
texts.1: SP set both boundary courses, one in the course selector window and one under the heading marker, but did not monitor whether the head of the bearing pointer stayed between them. The pointer reached the boundary course while altitude sat at the 300 foot limit of the tolerance. SP reversed toward the center of the wedge only after the IP called the bearing pointer position.
texts.2: SP set the pie in the sky references correctly but let the head of the bearing pointer approach the marked boundary during the maneuvering before checking it. The pointer came close to the head of the course arrow and altitude deviated about 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP recognized the trend on the EHSI and reversed back into the wedge with no prompting required.
texts.3: SP set one boundary course in the course selector window and marked the other with the heading marker, then kept the head of the bearing pointer between the two throughout the area work. Lateral containment was maintained with a usable margin on both sides and altitude was held inside 150 feet. The two references were rechecked whenever the working heading changed.
texts.4: SP applied the pie in the sky method with both boundaries marked before entering the area, and the head of the bearing pointer was kept well inside the sector at all times. Altitude deviations from the assigned block were of a few tens of feet only. The boundary references were maintained continuously without any need for reconstruction.
texts.marginal: SP kept both boundaries marked and stayed inside the sector, but the bearing pointer was repeatedly allowed to approach one of the two references before a reversal was started. The trend shows the marked boundary being treated as the turning point rather than as a limit. SP is expected to reverse while the pointer is still clear of the boundary course so that the sector is worked from its center.

texts_at.0: SP set the pie in the sky boundary references with the IP calling the position of the bearing pointer relative to the marked boundary through the maneuvering, due to first exposure to monitoring a bearing pointer against two set references at once. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to set and monitor the pie in the sky references independently on the next sortie, without the pointer position being called.
texts_at.1: SP set the pie in the sky boundary references to the level expected at this stage, with altitude deviation reaching about 300 feet, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the head of the bearing pointer being checked against the boundary less often than the maneuvering required. texts_at.2: SP recognized the trend on the EHSI and reversed back into the wedge with no prompting, correcting an altitude deviation of about 200 feet, due to the head of the bearing pointer being allowed to approach the marked boundary before it was checked. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reverse while the pointer is still comfortably clear of the boundary course, not once it has approached it.
texts_at.3: SP set one boundary course in the course selector window and marked the other with the heading marker, keeping the head of the bearing pointer between the two, altitude held inside about 150 feet, due to the two references being rechecked a beat after the working heading changed rather than at the same time. texts_above.4: SP applied the pie in the sky method with both boundaries marked before entering the area, the head of the bearing pointer kept well inside the sector at all times with altitude deviations of a few tens of feet, the boundary references maintained continuously without any need for reconstruction. error_modes.label: CONSTANT HEADING WITH BEARING POINTER ONLY AND DME RANGE

texts.0: SP maintained a constant heading and orientated on the bearing pointer alone, without crosschecking DME range. Because the radial position stayed satisfactory the increasing range went unnoticed and the aircraft flew out of the area along its length, with altitude also more than 300 feet out of the assigned block. IP intervened, called the DME and directed the turn back into the area.
texts.1: SP relied on the bearing pointer while holding a constant heading and checked DME only occasionally, so the range trend was not being tracked. The aircraft reached the range limit of the area with altitude at the 300 foot limit of the tolerance. SP turned to a heading that decreased DME only after the IP pointed out the range.
texts.2: SP held a constant heading for a full maneuver before including DME range in the crosscheck, so the range trend was recognized late. The aircraft closed to the far end of the area and altitude deviated some 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP turned toward the course, made the DME decrease and regained the working portion of the area without prompting.
texts.3: SP treated bearing and DME as a pair, changing heading as required so that the range stayed inside the area limits rather than holding one heading and watching the pointer alone. Position was maintained inside the boundaries with a working margin and altitude was held inside 150 feet. Range was checked at every maneuver setup.
texts.4: SP crosschecked bearing pointer and DME continuously and adjusted heading early so the range never approached the area limits. The aircraft was kept in the middle of the area in both radial and range terms and altitude deviations were of a few tens of feet. No range related correction was ever needed at short notice.
texts.marginal: SP included DME in the crosscheck and stayed within the area, but headings were held long enough for the range to build up before a correcting turn was flown. The trend is repeated recovery of range rather than continuous containment. SP is expected to adjust heading as soon as the range starts to trend toward the limit so that the correction remains small.

texts_at.0: SP crosschecked bearing pointer and DME with the IP calling the range each time the heading was held through a maneuver, due to first exposure to treating bearing and DME as a pair rather than reading the pointer alone. texts_at.1: SP treated bearing and DME as a pair to keep the aircraft inside the area limits to the level expected at this stage, with altitude deviation reaching about 300 feet, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to DME being included in the crosscheck later than the heading being held required. texts_at.2: SP turned toward the course, made the DME decrease and regained the working portion of the area without prompting, correcting an altitude deviation of about 200 feet, due to holding a constant heading for a full maneuver before including DME range in the crosscheck. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check DME range at the start of every maneuver, not only after it has been flown for a while.
texts_at.3: SP treated bearing and DME as a pair, changing heading as required so range stayed inside the area limits, altitude held inside about 150 feet, due to one range check being made a beat after the heading change that produced it rather than in anticipation. texts_above.3: SP treated bearing and DME as a pair, changing heading as required so the range stayed inside the area limits rather than holding one heading and watching the pointer alone, position maintained inside the boundaries with a working margin and altitude held inside about 110 feet. error_modes.label: GPS FLIGHT PLAN SELECTION FOR THE CLEARED FLIGHT AREA

texts.0: SP selected a GPS flight plan number that did not correspond to the flight area cleared for the sortie and then flew the boundaries depicted on Nav 5 as if they were the assigned ones. The displayed area was offset from the real one, so the aircraft was maneuvered outside the assigned limits with altitude also more than 300 feet out of the block. IP intervened, identified the wrong flight plan and repositioned the aircraft.
texts.1: SP loaded the flight plan for the area without verifying the number against the clearance and the IFG, so the displayed boundaries were only partially those of the assigned area. The aircraft was flown to the edge of the assigned area with altitude at the 300 foot limit of the tolerance. SP reselected the correct flight plan after the IP questioned the displayed area.
texts.2: SP initially selected the wrong flight plan number and did not select Nav 5 to confirm the depicted area before starting the maneuvering. The aircraft was worked toward one boundary and altitude deviated about 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP noticed that the depicted boundaries did not match the briefed area, reselected the correct flight plan and recovered the position unprompted.
texts.3: SP selected the flight plan number matching the cleared area in accordance with the IFG and displayed it on Nav 5 before entering the area. The depicted boundaries were verified against the clearance and the aircraft was kept inside them with a working margin, altitude held inside 150 feet.
texts.4: SP selected and verified the correct flight plan for the cleared area before area entry and kept the flight area displayed on Super Nav 5 throughout the sortie. Every maneuver was positioned in the working portion of the depicted area and altitude deviations were of a few tens of feet. The selection was confirmed again after any GPS page change.
texts.marginal: SP selected the correct flight plan and remained within the depicted area, but the verification against the clearance was done only once and the depicted boundaries were rarely referred to afterwards. The trend is an area picture accepted rather than actively used. SP is expected to keep the flight area displayed and to confirm the selection whenever the GPS display is changed.

texts_at.0: SP selected the GPS flight plan for the cleared area with the IP calling the flight plan number to verify against the clearance and the IFG, due to first exposure to confirming a selected flight plan number against a published reference before relying on the displayed boundaries. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to select and verify the flight plan independently on the next sortie, without the number being called.

texts.0: SP used the map mode with a range at which the area filled only a small part of the EHSI, so closure toward a boundary could not be resolved on the display. The developing drift was not seen at all and the aircraft crossed the boundary while altitude ran more than 300 feet out of the assigned block. IP intervened, reset the range and returned the aircraft to the assigned area.

The aircraft reached the edge of the area with altitude at the 300 foot limit of the tolerance. SP changed the range and turned back into the area after the IP prompted about the display setup.
texts.2: SP started the area work at an unsuitable map range and only later set the ARC map at 10 miles with Super Nav 5 at 20 miles, so the early boundary picture was coarse. The aircraft closed toward one boundary and altitude deviated some 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP reset the ranges and re-centered the aircraft in the area in good time.
texts.3: SP selected a range in EHSI map mode such that the area almost completely filled the display, with a larger range on the GPS control head to keep adjacent areas in view. Boundary distance was read directly off the display and the aircraft was kept inside the area with altitude held within 150 feet.
texts.4: SP set the ARC map at the 10 mile range with Super Nav 5 at the 20 mile range and adjusted the scale as the working position changed, so the area picture stayed optimal throughout. Lateral margins were generous at all times and altitude deviations were of a few tens of feet. No display reconfiguration was needed under time pressure.
texts.marginal: SP used a workable map range and stayed within the area, but the scale was left unchanged when the working position moved, so boundary distance was read from a less than optimal picture. The trend is a display setup that lags the tactical situation. SP is expected to adjust the map and control head ranges as the working position changes so the area picture remains fully resolved.

texts_at.0: SP selected the EHSI map and ARC range for the area display with the IP calling the range to set as the working position moved, due to first exposure to adjusting a display scale to match a changing working position rather than a fixed one. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to select and adjust the display ranges independently on the next sortie, without the range being called.
texts_at.1: SP selected a workable range in EHSI map mode to the level expected at this stage, with altitude deviation reaching about 300 feet, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the map scale being left unchanged as the working position moved within the area. error_modes.label: COMPOSITE CROSSCHECK OF GROUND REFERENCES AND INSTRUMENTS

texts.0: SP built area orientation on visual ground references alone and misidentified the road intersection being used as the boundary reference, with no instrument verification of the position. The false picture was maintained through the maneuvering and the aircraft ended up well outside the assigned area with altitude more than 300 feet out of the block. IP intervened to correct the orientation and reposition the aircraft.
texts.1: SP worked the area almost entirely head down on the navigation displays and did not verify the picture against cities, lakes and terrain, so the orientation was never confirmed by a composite crosscheck. The aircraft was flown to the edge of the area with altitude at the 300 foot limit of the tolerance. SP re-established the visual picture after the IP prompted for the ground references.
texts.2: SP delayed verifying the visual ground references against the GPS and VOR with DME after a reversal turn, so the position picture went briefly unconfirmed. The aircraft drifted toward the boundary and altitude deviated about 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP rebuilt the composite crosscheck, confirmed the position and corrected back into the area unprompted.
texts.3: SP used cities, lakes, road intersections and terrain as the primary means of area orientation and verified them against the GPS or VOR with DME throughout the sortie. The composite crosscheck kept the position picture continuously confirmed, the aircraft stayed inside the area and altitude was held within 150 feet.
texts.4: SP maintained a composite crosscheck in which visual ground references and instrument indications confirmed each other without interruption, so situational awareness was built rather than merely retained. The aircraft was kept in the working portion of the area at all times and altitude deviations were of a few tens of feet. Orientation was never in doubt at any point of the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP kept both visual and instrument references in use and stayed inside the area, but the two were checked in sequence with long gaps rather than as a single composite crosscheck. The trend is a position picture that is confirmed occasionally instead of continuously. SP is expected to verify ground references against the instruments as a routine so that any orientation error is caught while it is still small.

texts_at.0: SP built the composite crosscheck of ground references and instruments with the IP calling for the visual picture to be verified against the GPS or VOR with DME, due to first exposure to running a visual and an instrument check together rather than one after the other. error_modes.label: OPTIMUM ENERGY STATE FOR MANEUVERING WITHIN THE AREA BLOCK

texts.0: SP entered the maneuvering sequence far below the optimum energy state of 180 to 200 KIAS at an altitude midway between the top and bottom area limits, and made no deliberate energy gain before continuing. Entry airspeed was more than 20 knots low and the recovery took the aircraft more than 300 feet outside the assigned block. IP intervened, terminated the maneuver and reset the energy state.
texts.1: SP allowed the energy state to decay well away from the optimum band and started the next maneuver from the low side without a repositioning climb. Entry airspeed was about 20 knots below the optimum band and altitude sat at the 300 foot limit of the tolerance on recovery. SP climbed back toward the middle of the block only after the IP called the energy state.
texts.2: SP let the working altitude drift below the midpoint between the top and bottom area limits before addressing the energy state. Entry airspeed was some 15 knots below the optimum band and altitude deviated about 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP recognized the shortfall, flew a climb at 140 to 160 KIAS with MAX power and restored the working energy in good time.
texts.3: SP maintained an energy state close to 180 to 200 KIAS at an altitude midway between the top and bottom area limits, so each maneuver was entered from the intended block position. Airspeed at entry was held within 10 knots of the planned value and altitude within 150 feet of the assigned block.
texts.4: SP managed the energy state so that the aircraft was consistently at the optimum airspeed and midway between the area limits at every maneuver entry. Entry airspeeds were within a few knots of the planned values and altitude deviations from the block were of a few tens of feet. No repositioning climb or descent was needed for energy reasons.
texts.marginal: SP kept the energy state within acceptable limits, but the working altitude settled progressively toward the lower part of the block and entry airspeeds trended to the low side of the optimum band. The trend is a slow energy bleed that will eventually force a recovery near the bottom limit. SP is expected to restore the midpoint altitude and the optimum airspeed between maneuvers rather than after the margin is used up.

texts_at.0: SP set up the energy state for maneuvering within the area block with the IP calling the repositioning climb needed to restore the optimum band, due to first exposure to managing airspeed and altitude together as one energy state rather than as separate parameters. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to manage the energy state independently on the next sortie, without the repositioning climb being called.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the optimum energy state for maneuvering within the area block to the level expected at this stage, with entry airspeed about 20 knots below the optimum band and altitude about 300 feet from the block, due to the working altitude being allowed to drift toward the lower part of the block before it was addressed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to correct the working altitude toward the block midpoint as soon as it starts to drift, not once it has already drifted.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the shortfall, flew a climb at the briefed repositioning speed and power and restored the working energy in good time, correcting entry airspeed of about 15 knots low and altitude of about 200 feet, due to the working altitude drifting below the block midpoint before the energy state was addressed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check the working altitude against the block midpoint after every maneuver, not only when the shortfall has already built.
texts_at.3: SP maintained an energy state close to the optimum band at an altitude midway between the top and bottom area limits, entry airspeed held within about 10 knots and altitude within about 150 feet of the assigned block, due to one repositioning climb being started a beat later than the energy trend first suggested. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the repositioning climb the instant the energy trend is noticed, not a beat after.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the energy state for maneuvering within the area block, with entry airspeed about 18 knots below the optimum band and altitude about 270 feet from the block before a repositioning climb restored the working energy. The climb followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the working altitude drifting below the block midpoint, flew a climb at the briefed repositioning speed and power and restored the working energy in good time, entry airspeed held to about 15 knots low and altitude to about 200 feet, with no intervention. Checking the working altitude against the block midpoint after every maneuver, rather than only once the shortfall has built, would remove the correction from the area work. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent energy-state management.
texts_above.3: SP maintained an energy state close to the optimum band at an altitude midway between the top and bottom area limits, so each maneuver was entered from the intended block position, airspeed at entry held within about 8 knots and altitude within about 110 feet of the assigned block. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined energy-state management.
texts_above.4: SP managed the energy state so the aircraft was consistently at the optimum airspeed and midway between the area limits at every maneuver entry, entry airspeeds within two or three knots of the planned values and altitude deviations of a few tens of feet, no repositioning climb or descent needed for energy reasons. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless energy-state management.

error_modes.label: MANEUVER SEQUENCING BY ENERGY GAINERS AND ENERGY LOSERS

texts.0: SP sequenced consecutive energy losers, a Split-S followed by a cloverleaf and high G turns at low power, with no energy gainer interleaved and no plan for the exit energy of each maneuver. The aircraft was left so low on energy that trading about 1,000 feet of altitude for roughly 50 KIAS was attempted inside the block, taking it more than 300 feet outside the assigned altitudes and more than 20 knots off the required entry airspeed. IP intervened and stopped the sequence.
texts.1: SP flew the profile in the briefed order without accounting for the inherent energy losing properties of the individual maneuvers, so a deliberate energy change was required in the middle of the area work. Entry airspeed for the following maneuver was about 20 knots low and altitude sat at the 300 foot limit of the tolerance. SP reordered the remaining maneuvers only after the IP raised the energy state.
texts.2: SP planned the sequence loosely, so the exit airspeed of one maneuver did not match the entry airspeed required by the next. Entry airspeed was some 15 knots off and altitude deviated about 200 feet, between the 150 foot and 300 foot tolerance. SP recognized the mismatch, inserted an energy gainer and restored the profile without prompting.
texts.3: SP ordered the maneuvers so that the inherent energy properties of each were used, pairing energy losers with energy gainers and leaving the ELP stalls for the bottom of the area before RTB. Deliberate energy changes were largely unnecessary, entry airspeeds were within 10 knots of the planned values and altitude stayed within 150 feet of the block.
texts.4: SP sequenced the profile so that the exit airspeed of each maneuver was very close to the entry airspeed required by the next, and the energy losers were positioned at the end of the area work. Time and fuel spent on repositioning were minimal, entry airspeeds were within a few knots and altitude deviations of a few tens of feet. Energy state awareness was evident in every maneuver selection.
texts.marginal: SP flew a workable sequence and stayed within limits, but two energy losers were flown back to back and the resulting shortfall had to be made up with a dedicated climb. The trend is a profile that costs extra time and fuel in energy changes. SP is expected to select the next maneuver from the current energy state so that the sequence carries its own energy rather than requiring repair.

texts_at.0: SP sequenced the area maneuvers by their energy properties with the IP calling the exit airspeed of one maneuver to match against the entry requirement of the next, due to first exposure to planning a sequence around the inherent energy gain or loss of each maneuver. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to sequence the maneuvers by energy properties independently on the next sortie, without the airspeed match being called.
texts_at.1: SP ordered the maneuvers by their energy properties to the level expected at this stage, with entry airspeed for the following maneuver about 20 knots off and altitude about 300 feet from the block, due to the exit airspeed of one maneuver not being checked against the entry requirement of the next before the sequence was flown. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the exit airspeed of each maneuver against the entry requirement of the next before flying the sequence, not after.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the mismatch, inserted an energy gainer and restored the profile without prompting, correcting entry airspeed of about 15 knots and altitude of about 200 feet, due to the sequence being planned loosely so the exit airspeed of one maneuver did not match the entry airspeed the next required. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to plan the exit-to-entry airspeed match for the whole sequence before the area work begins.
texts_at.3: SP ordered the maneuvers so the inherent energy properties of each were used, pairing energy losers with energy gainers, entry airspeeds within about 10 knots of the planned values and altitude within about 150 feet of the block, due to one pairing being adjusted a beat after the mismatch first appeared rather than planned in advance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to plan every pairing in advance rather than adjusting one after a mismatch appears.

texts_above.1: SP sequenced the area maneuvers by their energy properties, with entry airspeed for the following maneuver about 18 knots off and altitude about 270 feet from the block before an energy gainer was inserted and the profile restored. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a mismatch between the exit airspeed of one maneuver and the entry airspeed the next required, inserted an energy gainer and restored the profile without prompting, entry airspeed held to about 15 knots and altitude to about 200 feet, no intervention needed. Planning the exit-to-entry airspeed match for the whole sequence before the area work begins, rather than inserting a gainer after a mismatch appears, would remove the correction from the profile. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good maneuver-sequencing technique.
texts_above.3: SP ordered the maneuvers so the inherent energy properties of each were used, pairing energy losers with energy gainers and leaving the ELP stalls for the bottom of the area before RTB, deliberate energy changes largely unnecessary, entry airspeeds within about 8 knots and altitude within about 110 feet of the block. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good maneuver-sequencing technique.
texts_above.4: SP sequenced the profile so the exit airspeed of each maneuver was very close to the entry airspeed required by the next, energy losers positioned at the end of the area work, entry airspeeds within a few knots and altitude deviations of a few tens of feet, energy-state awareness evident in every maneuver selection. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent maneuver-sequencing technique.
